high_priority_articles.title: Germany’s Defense Shift: Merz, NATO, And Rearmament – Analysis - Eurasia Review
high_priority_articles.summary: Germany’s Defense Shift: Merz, NATO, And Rearmament – Analysis  Eurasia Review
high_priority_articles.full_text:
By Dr. Emily Holland
Key Takeaways:
- Chancellor Merz has committed Germany to 5 percent of GDP defense spending, a 25 percent troop increase by 2031 and roughly €215 billion annually by 2035, exempt from the debt brake.
- Implementation faces resistance from travel-restriction rules, low recruitment (only 530 enlistees from a major drive) and rising conscientious-objector applications.
- While 40 percent of Germans want more defense spending and 66 percent view NATO favorably, strong AfD gains in eastern states on pro-Russia platforms complicate building the needed political and societal consensus.
(FPRI) — When newly elected German Chancellor Friedrich Merz delivered his first major address to the Bundestag in May 2025, following a closely fought election that ultimately saw Merz’s CDU (Christian Democratic Union) forge an alliance with the SPD (Socialist Democratic Party of Germany), the subject of rearmament increased in importance for his party’s agenda.
Merz’s pledge to build the “strongest conventional army in Europe”[1] marked a turning point for domestic and foreign policy alike, and was met with some resistance across the Republic. Nearly 80 years after the conclusion of World War II, and close to 40 after the country’s reunification, major reinvestment in defense remains a delicate issue in Berlin’s fractious political landscape, as well as in the public conversation.
However, with the Russia-Ukraine war continuing just 1500km from the country’s eastern borders, and America’s historical support of NATO uncertain once again under a re-elected Trump administration, Merz had undoubtedly taken advantage of a prescient moment in his attempt to shift the national conversation.
Merz’s pledge that Germany spend a total of 5 percent of GDP on defense, meeting the demands of NATO secretary Mark Rutte,[2] was equaled in ambition by a commitment to increase troop numbers by up to 25 percent by 2031, as well as sweeping replacements of aging tanks, aircraft, and ships. Estimated spending on defense is estimated to reach €215 billion ($242 billion) by 2035, a result of military funding now being exempted from the country’s “debt-brake,” a rigid constitutional rule limiting net borrowing. First established by Angela Merkel in 2009, it was unpicked by her CDU successor, in deeply controversial reforms that followed Merz’s victory in 2025.
Despite the neighboring conflicts and rapidly shifting political realities cited as the foundation for this comparatively radical shift in priorities for Germany, the evidence in the 15 months since suggests that Merz may struggle to achieve his ambitions while in office. There has been progress; his partners in the SPD, traditionally a party averse to defense investment, now largely share Merz’s perspective.[3]
And while the tangible, public effects of the Russia-Ukraine war seen in 2022, such as chilled public swimming pools to save on gas,[4] may have faded into memory, the threat of Russia’s aggression continues to make itself known. In August 2026, a drone carrying explosives was intercepted at Leipzig airport,[5] an incident widely accepted in the media to be an act of sabotage directed by Moscow.
Polling by YouGov as recently as July 2026[6] suggests that 40 percent of German citizens believe the government is spending “too little” on defense and security, while 24 percent feel that the expenditure is “about the right amount” and a further 17 percent believe the country is spending too much. Meanwhile, 66 percent of citizens have a broadly favorable view of NATO as an organization, a figure greater than the approval for other major international organizations, including the United Nations (54 percent) and the European Union (60 percent).
Nonetheless, the measures proposed by the parliament to redress this perceived imbalance have sometimes proved challenging in a country with a still fragile relationship with its military history, and where mandatory conscription was only suspended in 2011. A national scandal erupted in April 2026, when it became known that legislation had passed featuring a clause that all German men between 17 and 45 are required to seek permission from the armed forces should they wish to leave Germany for work or travel purposes totaling more than three months of absence.[7] The change had not been publicly communicated by the Bundestag, nor the Bundeswehr, discovered only in fine print by journalists some months following its legally binding introduction.
Amid much confusion, a spokesperson quickly clarified that the change was made only in anticipation of a potential return to conscription, stressing that, “the regulation already applied during the Cold War and had no practical relevance; in particular, it is not subject to sanction.”[8] But the news triggered a fresh wave of alarm. Only a month earlier, 50,000 German schoolchildren walked out of schools nationwide,[9] a swiftly organized response to the more widely communicated news that all male German citizens born after 2008 will undergo a medical exam determining their fitness to serve. In Berlin, children waved placards that addressed the chancellor directly: “Friedrich Merz to the front.”[10]
In 2024, the German military consisted of approximately 186,000 active military members in the Bundeswehr, including around 64,000 active soldiers and a further 81,000 civilian personnel.[11]
As well as legal changes made to anticipate expanded manpower in the German military, attempts at a more direct recruitment drive have also taken place. Throughout the first half of 2026, the Bundeswehr distributed more than 300,000 questionnaires to young Germans, including 153,200 to men, who were legally obliged to respond. Despite a 96 percent response rate, as well as one in five asked reporting an interest in a role in military service, the enrollment rate associated with the campaign was just 530 people by the end of June 2026.[12]
News of this meagre figure proved a significant nexus of conversation across the German media. Underscoring what the press described as an emerging generational divide, it was revealed weeks later that the number of German men seeking the status of conscientious objector, a fundamental right in Germany’s post-war constitution when based on either moral or religious grounds, had reached a greater number of applications in the previous six months than the entirety of 2025; 5,862, versus 3,879. In the case of a wider, more critical conflict, this fundamental right could prove challenging to recruitment, even with a legally mandated draft.
In parallel, the Bundeswehr has attempted to render military service more appealing to young people within the context of a challenging German economy, which is currently stagnating for the seventh consecutive year, despite a slight, resilient GDP growth of 0.2 percent reported in Q2 of 2026. Rising costs associated with healthcare, pensions, and travel loom over the everyday finances of young Germans. New recruits are promised a base salary of €2,600 before tax, free train travel, and a subsidized driver’s license. The current minimum wage in Germany is €13.90 per hour, which translates to roughly €2,400 gross per month.[13]
These figures are not particularly competitive in comparison to Germany’s private sector. However, the career does offer the promise of professional stability and security, something reaffirmed by the direction in which Merz is driving the military sector.
Germany’s history as a divided state, as well as its geographic location, has resulted in an anxiety concerning Russia that runs deeper than in some other Northern European countries. Since the onset of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Germany has welcomed more than 1.2 million Ukrainian refugees,[14] each able to access standard social welfare, healthcare, and integration programs.[15] This wave of migration has proven less controversial than Merkel’s decision to welcome a similar number of Syrian refugees in 2015, a decision Merz is attempting to reverse, claiming in March 2026 that 80 percent of these individuals will be expected to return to their home country within three years.[16]
Although both cultural and security issues could be cited as differentiating these two migrations, the hosting of Ukrainian refugees instead provided a moment of shared purpose and pride, with spontaneous gatherings of Berliners waiting at train stations to provide shelter for fleeing citizens. These unifying images provided a template for a compassionate politics amongst Germans, standing against the brutality of what was emerging across the continent.
Still, the unique political landscape of a reunified Germany will call for a more targeted and nuanced approach in communicating the importance of defense. Traditionally, many voters in the former East Germany favor a more dialogue-focused approach to Russian relations, rather than military engagement or investment, retaining generational skepticism towards the transatlantic relationship with the United States, as well as NATO.
Since their foundation in 2013, the far-right AfD (Alternative für Deutschland) have consistently made notable gains in both local and national election cycles. In July 2026, the party’s overall support in eastern states such as Saxony, Thuringia, and Brandenburg tracked between 36 percent and 41 percent, contributing a nationwide figure of 41 percent support.[17] In Saxony-Anhalt on September 6, the AfD won 43.8 percent of the vote, more than doubling its 2021 result, while the CDU fell to 17.2 percent, its worst-ever result in the state. Two weeks later, the AfD also finished first in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania with 38.2 percent, while the CDU won just 4.9 percent and, for the first time in its post-war history, failed to enter a state parliament. high_priority_articles.title: Lula Wins Brazil’s Runoff: Will Trump Escalate Tariffs and Sanctions? - Diplomacy and Law
high_priority_articles.summary: Lula Wins Brazil’s Runoff: Will Trump Escalate Tariffs and Sanctions?  Diplomacy and Law
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Lula's victory in Brazil's October 25, 2026, presidential runoff has renewed attention to the Lula–Trump tariffs dispute and the possibility of further American sanctions. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defeated Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, securing a fourth, nonconsecutive presidential term after a campaign marked by disagreements over Brazil's relations with Washington. The election comes after Donald Trump's administration imposed substantial tariffs on Brazilian exports and previously sanctioned Supreme Federal Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes. The immediate question is whether Washington will increase economic pressure following Lula's reelection.
Trump retains legal instruments to impose additional tariffs, expand existing trade restrictions, or introduce new targeted sanctions. Lula's electoral victory, however, does not independently satisfy the statutory conditions for using those instruments. Any further measures would require decisions under applicable American legislation, while their international legality would depend on the specific obligations governing trade, economic coercion, and relations between sovereign states.
The dispute already extends beyond political disagreement. Brazil has initiated two proceedings against American tariffs at the World Trade Organization (WTO), including a July 2026 complaint challenging the Section 301 duties. Meanwhile, a February 2026 ruling of the U.S. Supreme Court restricted presidential authority to impose tariffs under emergency economic legislation. Bilateral negotiations have nevertheless continued, creating an alternative to further restrictions. Lula's reelection leaves Washington and Brasília facing an established trade confrontation, unresolved legal proceedings, and competing incentives for economic cooperation.
1. Lula’s Reelection and Washington’s Immediate Response
Lula's reelection preserves the Brazilian executive's existing foreign-policy leadership during a difficult period in U.S.–Brazil relations. The relationship deteriorated following American tariff measures and disagreements concerning decisions by Brazilian judicial authorities. Questions involving trade regulation, political expression, and the prosecution of Jair Bolsonaro became entangled with economic policy, producing disputes that were already underway before the presidential campaign ended.
The election also carried diplomatic significance because Flávio Bolsonaro belonged to a political family with established connections to Trump and his political movement. A change of government in Brasília could have altered the political environment surrounding those disputes, although the applicable legal obligations would not have disappeared automatically. Lula's victory leaves negotiations in the hands of an administration that has consistently rejected the justification for the American Section 301 tariffs.
Washington's response must be distinguished from the political significance of the result. Criticism of Lula, expressions of sympathy for the Bolsonaro family, and formal decisions affecting Brazilian commerce have different consequences. The relevant evidence of escalation would be a new governmental measure, rather than an inference drawn from political relationships.
1.1 The Runoff Result and Lula’s Fourth Presidential Term
Brazil held its presidential runoff on October 25, 2026, after neither leading candidate obtained an absolute majority of valid votes in the first round. On October 4, Flávio Bolsonaro received 56,104,503 votes, or 47.03%, while Lula obtained 53,879,538 votes, or 45.16%, according to the completed first-round results published by the Superior Electoral Court, known as the Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE). Bolsonaro entered the runoff ahead by approximately 2.22 million votes.
Lula reversed that result on October 25. The TSE's near-complete election-night returns placed him at approximately 51.8% of valid votes against 48.2% for Bolsonaro, with a lead approaching 4.4 million votes. The Associated Press subsequently reported the result after counting had been completed, confirming Lula's reelection. The figures establish the reversal of the first-round outcome without treating an earlier election-night snapshot as the exact final total.
The determination of the electoral winner is distinct from formal certification, known in Brazilian electoral law as diplomação. That procedure follows the rules established by the TSE and confirms the elected candidates' entitlement to assume office, subject to the applicable legal requirements. Constitutional Amendment No. 111/2021 changed the presidential inauguration date to January 5, beginning with the mandate resulting from the 2026 election. Lula's fourth term is consequently scheduled to begin on January 5, 2027.
The runoff was accompanied by controversy after Supreme Federal Court Justice Cristiano Zanin ordered an extension of voting amid difficulties involving transportation and severe weather. The TSE clarified on October 25 that voting would continue only where polling had not already closed at 5 p.m. The tribunal also stated that the receipt of polling-station records, totalization, and publication of results would resume after 7 p.m.
Any legal challenge arising from that decision falls within the jurisdiction of Brazil's competent electoral and judicial institutions. A controversy over voting procedures does not itself establish fraud or invalidate a presidential election. Under Article 77 of the Brazilian Constitution, the national electoral outcome is determined through Brazil's constitutional and electoral processes, not through recognition or approval by a foreign government.
1.2 Trump, the Bolsonaro Family, and the Election Result
Trump's relationship with the Bolsonaro family has influenced the political environment surrounding bilateral disputes. During Jair Bolsonaro's presidency, the two leaders developed close public ties and expressed overlapping positions on several international and domestic issues. Their association continued after Bolsonaro left office, while American criticism of Brazilian judicial proceedings became increasingly prominent during Trump's second presidency.
In October 2026, Reuters reported concerns among foreign diplomats in Brasília about possible American involvement in the political consequences of a closely contested election. Those concerns reflected the unusual diplomatic circumstances surrounding the runoff, but they did not establish that the United States had adopted a policy of rejecting Lula's victory. A reported fear of foreign interference remains different from evidence that the feared action occurred.
Trump's public statements immediately before the result were comparatively restrained. Questioned on October 25 about his position toward the candidates, he said the United States was monitoring the election without declaring support for either candidate in that exchange. Earlier political expressions concerning the Bolsonaro family provide relevant context, but they cannot establish a subsequent decision to impose economic penalties.
The legal significance of Lula's victory lies in the continuity of Brazil's elected government and its existing policy positions. The United States has no supervisory jurisdiction over the TSE, and its political preferences do not determine who holds Brazil's presidency. Washington nevertheless retains considerable influence over bilateral trade and financial relations through instruments governed by American law. Those powers, rather than any authority over Brazil's electoral process, form the basis of the potential economic confrontation.
2. The Lula–Trump Tariffs Already Affecting Brazil
The current trade confrontation cannot be explained through a single tariff percentage. Since 2025, Washington has employed several legal authorities to restrict imports, including emergency economic legislation and provisions of the Trade Act of 1974. Some measures were directed specifically at Brazil; others applied to numerous trading partners. Their rates, exemptions, and legal consequences differ.
The distinction became particularly significant in February 2026, when the Supreme Court rejected the administration's interpretation of its emergency tariff powers. The judgment led to the termination of duties imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), including the Brazil-specific restrictions adopted in July 2025. Separate tariff measures under Sections 232 and 301 remained unaffected.
By the time Lula won reelection, the principal Brazil-specific trade restrictions arose from the July 2026 Section 301 investigation. Their application depends on the products imported, the relevant exemptions, and the relationship between overlapping duties. Assessing the prospect of further escalation requires first establishing the restrictions that were already operating.
2.1 The 2025 Tariffs and the Supreme Court’s Intervention
On July 30, 2025, Trump signed Executive Order 14323, Addressing Threats to the United States by the Government of Brazil. The order imposed an additional 40% ad valorem duty on covered Brazilian imports under IEEPA, subject to exemptions and subsequent modifications. Together with previously applicable emergency tariff measures, the order initially produced a headline additional rate of 50% for certain Brazilian products.
The administration justified its action partly through allegations concerning Brazilian judicial proceedings, restrictions on political expression, and the treatment of American technology companies. Those allegations formed part of the executive's stated rationale for declaring an emergency. Their inclusion in a presidential order did not independently establish the legality of imposing customs duties under IEEPA.

high_priority_articles.title: Thailand welcomes US-Myanmar engagement, expects ASEAN talks on country’s future - Y100 WNCY
high_priority_articles.summary: Thailand welcomes US-Myanmar engagement, expects ASEAN talks on country’s future  Y100 WNCY
high_priority_articles.full_text:
By Sergio Goncalves and Miguel Pereira
LISBON, Oct 23 (Reuters) – Thailand welcomes US engagement with Myanmar and expects discussions at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations’ November summit in Manila on how to proceed with the member barred since the 2021 coup, Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow told Reuters on Friday.
The United States and Myanmar’s military-backed government held talks in Tokyo two weeks ago, their second meeting in a month as Washington steps up re-engagement with the generals it shunned after the coup.
“We don’t want to see Myanmar isolated, we don’t want Myanmar to be an arena for geopolitical rivalry … so the US engagement is something that we welcome,” he said.
Engagement “does not mean legitimizing the regime,” but aims to encourage peaceful conflict resolution and reconciliation with the opposition, Sihasak, who is also deputy prime minister, added.
He said there was “some shift in ASEAN’s position,” citing Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing’s recent visits to Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, Thailand and Malaysia, but said it was unclear whether the Manila summit would address restoring Myanmar’s full representation.
“It’s good that we’re going to have a very substantive, very extensive, and very in-depth discussion on how to proceed on Myanmar,” he said.
He also said Thailand and Cambodia could resolve their longstanding land and maritime boundary disputes within 12 to 18 months despite limited progress.
“It is possible, everything is possible,” he said, cautioning that confidence-building and addressing security concerns along the land border, where clashes have occurred, must come first.
Cambodia launched a conciliation process under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea in June to resolve the maritime boundary dispute, after Thailand terminated a 2001 joint development framework in May following deadly border clashes. The first meeting was held about a month ago.
“Right now, we haven’t achieved, to be very frank, much progress,” he said.
The maritime dispute centers on overlapping claims to about 26,000 sq km in the Gulf of Thailand, believed to hold oil and gas reserves worth around $300 billion. Thailand wants the boundary defined before discussing resource-sharing, he said.
Thailand-EU free-trade talks are in their final stage and could conclude by year-end if there is mutual political will, he added.
(Reporting by Sergio Goncalves and Miguel Pereira in Lisbon; Editing by Matthew Lewis)

high_priority_articles.title: India-EU FTA timeline brings MedTech tariff relief closer for hospitals - Medical Buyer
high_priority_articles.summary: India-EU FTA timeline brings MedTech tariff relief closer for hospitals  Medical Buyer
high_priority_articles.full_text:
India’s healthcare sector now has a clearer view of when lower-cost European medical equipment and medicines could reach its hospitals and supply chains. The India-European Union Free Trade Agreement, announced on January 27, 2026, is expected to be signed before the end of 2026 and could come into force by March or April 2027, once approval and ratification procedures are complete on both sides.
The timeline matters for healthcare procurement teams because the EU is a major source of advanced medical technology for India. European exports to India already include medical and optical instruments alongside machinery, transport equipment, and chemicals, and the agreement is designed to cut both tariffs and administrative barriers on this trade.
Deep cuts on equipment duties
The most consequential provisions for hospitals and diagnostic providers concern capital equipment and devices. Indian import duties on medical and surgical equipment, which currently run as high as 27.5 percent, would fall to zero across 90 percent of the relevant tariff lines. For high-value purchases such as imaging systems, surgical platforms, and critical care equipment, the removal of duties at that level would materially lower landed costs. 																
															
Medicines and device inputs are also covered. Indian tariffs on European pharmaceuticals and chemicals, currently as high as 11 percent and 22 percent respectively, would move to zero, along with duties on plastics and related industrial inputs used in device components. The input-side cuts are relevant to domestic manufacturers that source specialized polymers and chemicals from Europe for consumables and device housings.
The scale of import dependence gives these changes added weight. India relies on imports for a large majority of its medical devices, with estimates placing that share at 70 to 90 percent, which means tariff reductions flow quickly into hospital budgets, tender pricing, and distributor margins.
Export opportunity for Indian drugmakers and device makers
The benefits run in both directions. The agreement opens access to a USD 572.3 billion EU pharmaceuticals and medical-devices market and includes liberalized tariffs for India-made medical devices intended to accelerate growth in the sector. Europe remains a large but under-penetrated destination for Indian drugmakers, with the EU accounting for about 19 percent of India’s pharmaceutical exports despite India’s position as a leading global supplier of generic medicines. 																
															
Market access, however, depends on more than tariffs. European regulatory requirements for medicines and devices remain demanding, and Indian manufacturers will need certification, quality systems, and documentation aligned with EU standards to convert lower duties into actual sales. Exchanging information on product standards and pricing ahead of implementation has been identified as an early step for companies on both sides.
Approval process and the road to 2027
The agreement is now in its final institutional stretch. The European Commission submitted its proposals on September 11, 2026, and Council approval would clear the way for signing, after which the European Parliament must give its consent and India must complete its own procedures. Negotiations stretched over nearly two decades, though most of the final progress came in the past 13 months. 																
															
The wider trade relationship provides a substantial base. Bilateral merchandise trade between India and the EU stood at USD 136.54 billion in 2024-25, with Indian exports of USD 75.85 billion and imports of USD 60.68 billion.
The agreement also sharpens a policy balance for India’s MedTech sector. Healthcare providers and procurement bodies stand to gain from lower landed costs on European equipment as tariffs phase down, creating a trade-off between import substitution goals and near-term affordability. Domestic makers of devices, consumables, and diagnostics are likely to face sharper price competition from European suppliers, even as the same agreement widens their access to one of the world’s largest healthcare markets.
MB Bureau

high_priority_articles.title: Saudi Arabia intercepts Houthi missiles, drones as Yemen fighting continues - Iran International
high_priority_articles.summary: Saudi Arabia intercepts Houthi missiles, drones as Yemen fighting continues  Iran International
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia intercepted drones and missiles over Riyadh and southern parts of the country on Sunday as fighting with Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis continued, the Saudi-led coalition said.
The coalition said two drones and a ballistic missile were launched toward Riyadh, while a cruise missile targeted Khamis Mushait in the south. It later said 10 ballistic missiles aimed at southern Saudi Arabia had also been intercepted.
Saudi civil defense authorities issued emergency alerts for Riyadh, Abha and Khamis Mushait before later saying the danger had passed.
Houthis threaten Riyadh airport
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport remained a “military target” and warned airlines, airport staff and travelers against using it.
The airport resumed operations at two terminals on Sunday after an October 10 attack, which the Houthis said they carried out, killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.
The Houthis also said they attacked the airport and Saudi oil facilities on Saturday. Saudi authorities did not directly confirm those assertions.
Fighting intensifies around Red Sea routes
Saudi Arabia has stepped up strikes against the Houthis after the group seized territory along Yemen’s Red Sea coast last month, bringing the fighting closer to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a major global shipping route.
The renewed conflict has broken a UN-brokered truce that had largely held since 2022.
Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen’s civil war in 2015 at the head of a coalition backing the internationally recognized government after the Houthis seized Sanaa the previous year.

high_priority_articles.title: Houthi attacks rock Riyadh when Saudi Arabia reopens airport
high_priority_articles.summary: Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia continued Sunday, rocking capital Riyadh as it prepared to reopen its international airport. Saudi Arabia, which leads a military coalition fighting...
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia continued Sunday, rocking capital Riyadh as it prepared to reopen its international airport.
Saudi Arabia, which leads a military coalition fighting the Iran-backed Houthis, has faced a barrage of strikes from the group in recent weeks.
The fighting erupted after a yearslong truce between the Houthis and Yemen's Riyadh-backed government fell apart.
Riyadh's international airport said flights would resume Sunday after a two-week closure following the Houthi strikes. However, it remained unclear to what extent the airport was operational.
The Houthi fighters have carried out waves of strikes on the airport, including an attack this month that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade.
The group has also targeted oil infrastructure and other sites, with the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen announcing Sunday it had intercepted 10 Houthi missiles fired at southern Saudi Arabia.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree warned that Riyadh airport was still "unsafe" and a "military target."
"The Yemeni Armed Forces warn all international, regional and local airlines – as well as staff and travelers – against using King Khalid Airport in Riyadh, as it is unsafe and serves as a military target for our forces," he said.
"The Saudi regime shall bear the consequences of any operations at the airport."
An AFP journalist in the city heard three explosions in the early hours of Sunday, with residents receiving alert messages for a "hostile aerial threat" urging them to stay in a safe place.
The warning came as the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it had downed a ballistic missile launched by the group towards Riyadh, as well as two drones in the capital area.
"Air defenses intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward Riyadh," the coalition posted on X.
Later Sunday morning, the coalition said its forces intercepted a cruise missile fired by the Houthis at the kingdom's southern city of Khamis Mushait.
Attacks appeared to target areas across the south, with warnings also issued for Abha city and Namas Governorate.
"The bombardment has been very heavy since this morning – may God keep us safe. Everything is shaking because of the explosions," one resident in Khamis Mushait said Sunday on condition of anonymity.
The attacks came after the Houthi fighters said that – in the space of 24 hours – they targeted three Saudi airports, including in Riyadh, energy installations, a pipeline and an air base.
The Saudi civil defense agency said it had also responded to falling debris in the Mecca and Medina regions on Saturday after intercepting two Houthi missiles.
The Houthis denied targeting the cities, the two holiest in Islam, calling the Saudi claim a "huge lie."
The Houthis also fired at the southern Yemeni city of Aden, the interim seat of the Saudi-backed government, saying they targeted a naval base and military camp overseen by Saudi forces.
The flare-up in Yemen, with the Houthis taking control of the entire Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive last month, has further destabilized the region and disrupted oil markets.
The Houthi attacks have dealt a blow to Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest exporter of crude, disrupting businesses, airlines and residents, and rattling its drive to shift its international image.

high_priority_articles.full_text:
Europe should be included in discussions on a peace settlement in Ukraine because its position could be crucial, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov said on Sunday.
The U.S. has been unable to put pressure on Kyiv to agree to a peace deal, Ushakov said in an interview with state television correspondent Pavel Zarubin.
“Before, it seemed after Anchorage, that the U.S. administration might be able to dictate something and force Kyiv to comply. But so far, this hasn't really worked out,” Ushakov said, referring to a 2025 meeting in Alaska between U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“That's because it's not enough to talk only to Kyiv; we need to talk to the whole of Europe, which fully supports Kyiv.”
EU HAS MADE CAUTIOUS APPROACHES
After initially leaving it to Trump to try to broker an end to Russia's war in Ukraine, the EU has made cautious approaches to Russia. The leaders of Britain, Germany and France have said they supported a proposal for talks between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Putin to try to secure a ceasefire, and that Europe would play a role.
Russia, meanwhile, has said it would be open to dialogue but not ultimatums.
On Sunday, Ushakov said that Russia was ready to resume three-way peace talks with Ukraine and the U.S. after Russia's National Unity Day on Nov. 4, echoing Kremlin comments this week on Putin's willingness to resume U.S.-mediated talks with Ukraine as soon as next month.
Zelensky said on Friday that peace negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the U.S. had agreed to meet at a technical level in the first half of November in Abu Dhabi, adding that he hoped a meeting of their leaders would follow.
Ushakov also commented on a potential meeting between Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump, saying that preparations had already started. The proposed meeting is set to be held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China over Nov. 18-19.
A separate meeting between Putin and Trump in Shenzhen had not been agreed upon, Ushakov said.

high_priority_articles.title: Indonesia begins trimming pipeline gas exports to Singapore - The Star
high_priority_articles.summary: Indonesia begins trimming pipeline gas exports to Singapore  The Star
high_priority_articles.full_text:
JAKARTA: Indonesia is reducing natural gas exports to neighbouring Singapore as President Prabowo Subianto seeks to shore up domestic supply and strengthen energy security for South-East Asia’s largest economy.
Pipeline gas deliveries to the city-state were being cut by about 31 million standard cubic feet per day to help bolster domestic energy generation, said Djoko Siswanto, who leads SKK Migas, the government agency overseeing Indonesia’s upstream oil and gas industry.
The cuts are equivalent to about 14% of Indonesia’s average pipeline-gas exports to Singapore last year, according to Bloomberg calculations based on energy ministry data compiled from SKK Migas reports.
Singapore’s Energy Market Authority (EMA) said in an emailed statement that the country had sufficient energy supplies.
The reduction is expected to be over a period of 18 days, and represents less than 2% of total daily gas demand, according to the EMA.
Indonesia is the biggest supplier of gas to Singapore, which depends on the imported fuel for nearly all of its power generation.
“We have contingency plans in place to deal with such reductions,” the EMA said last Saturday. Singapore GasCo is ready to import more liquefied natural gas (LNG) at any time, the EMA said.
SKK Migas’ Siswanto said in a text message that 15 million scfd sourced from Natuna would be diverted to a state utility unit in Batam, a data-centre and tourism hub.
Meanwhile, 16 million scfd from Sumatra would go toward supporting electricity needs in Batam, Bintan and Sumatra.
Local media reports earlier cited Djoko as saying last Friday that the cuts don’t affect any other country. The reduction was effective last Saturday.
Singapore’s Gas Supply Pte, which imports gas from Indonesia, said it’s already seeing an impact.
“Delivery of gas to our customers has been affected by temporary reductions in supply from our upstream supplier in Indonesia,” a Gas Supply spokesperson said in an email last Saturday, adding the company is engaging with its supplier and customers to manage the situation.
Sembcorp Gas Pte, another importer of Indonesia gas, didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment outside of regular business hours.
While Indonesia is a major gas exporter, overseas shipments have declined in recent years as a growing share of output is directed to domestic use.
Major LNG markets include China, Japan and South Korea, while pipeline natural gas is sent to Singapore and Malaysia.
A 16-hour blackout in Batam earlier this month, affecting more than 411,000 customers, has made Indonesia’s move to divert more gas toward domestic electricity generation more prescient.
The government replaced the chief executive of state-owned electricity giant PT Perusahaan Listrik Negara following the outage.
Prabowo this week stressed the importance of safeguarding Indonesia’s natural resources and prioritising domestic needs in a wide-ranging speech to cabinet members.
He also touched on regional haze, the threat of a market downgrade by MSCI Inc and the progress of his administration two years into his five-year term.
Speaking after the address, Coordinating Minister for Downstreaming and Energy Transition Bahlil Lahadalia echoed the president’s call for economic self-reliance and suggested Indonesia could curb gas exports to “neighbouring countries”.
“If other countries have a different view of us, they should be careful,” he told reporters.
“I, for one, might consider not extending gas exports to neighbouring countries –because, after all, we are in survival mode and must prioritise meeting our own domestic needs.” — Bloomberg

high_priority_articles.summary: US Interest Rate Forecast: Oil Rally Fuels December Fed Hike Risks  FXEmpireUs Federal Reserve Interest Rates: US Fed expected to hold rates as inflation, energy costs weigh ahead of midterms  The Times of IndiaFederal Reserve preview: A pause before a December hike  ing thinkFed expected to hold rates steady days ahead of US midterms  Yahoo Finance UKWeek Ahead for FX, Bonds: Decisions From Fed, Other Central Banks in Focus  WSJ
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The surge in oil prices and strong AI spending increase the cost for businesses and keep inflation high. The persistent inflation keeps the door open for further increases in the interest rate. The market now watches for the next employment and inflation data to further understand the next move in the US Treasury yields. In my view, the next move in the US dollar will depend on the change in the expectations for interest rates. This article presents the outlook for interest rates and the key levels to understand the next move in US dollar, EURUSD and GBPUSD.
US Interest Rate Forecast: December Hike Risks Remain in Focus
The market expects the Fed to keep interest rates at 3.75%-4% in October but expectations of rate hike in December are high due to persistent inflation and high oil prices.
The energy market disruptions in the Middle East have impacted the US Treasury market. US Treasury yields have continued to rally higher, but the momentum is slowing in October. However, the recent trend suggests that the 10-year US Treasury yields may continue to go up towards the 6% level or beyond. The weakness in employment, slow growth and the drop in inflation may limit the current strength in US Treasury yields.
The chart below shows that the 10-year US Treasury yield dropped from 5.37% towards the key support level of the 50-day SMA near the 5% area. The yield is now consolidating around this support and looks to rally higher again.
The MOVE index is high but not that extremely high. The chart below shows that the MOVE Index currently remains below the warning level of 120. A break above the 120 level would increase the risk of surge to the 150 area. This may bring additional volatility in the Treasury market.
The Fed started to purchase short term Treasury securities in December 2025 when the liquidity issues arrived. These operations help the Fed to control interest rates in the short term and support the functionality of the market.
Inflation currently remains above the Fed’s 2% target. The Fed is trying to keep repo markets and Treasury markets liquid enough to function via ample reserves.
AI Spending Raises Inflation Risks as Factory Construction Slows
The construction boom in data centers and power infrastructure has been so significant that it might be crowding out some other sectors. It does not mean that the other sectors are not receiving capital, but it means that the strong demand for electricity, workers and construction materials may increase the cost for other businesses and increase the pressure on inflation.
This weakness can be seen in the construction of manufacturing facilities. The construction of manufacturing dropped significantly from the peak of $250,233 million in 2024 to $170,339 million in 2026. This highlights weakness in other parts of business investment.
US Dollar Forecast: 100.50 Support Shapes the Next Move
Support at 100.50 Keep Path Open to 104
The outlook for US Dollar Index will depend on how expectations for the Fed change compared with expectations for other central banks. If the market expects more restrictive outlook for US rate relative to Europe and the UK, the US dollar may strengthen against these currencies. This may increase pressure on EUR/USD and GBP/USD. But strong expectations for interest rates in Europe and UK will provide support for the euro and the pound.
The chart below shows that the US Dollar Index has been trading within the ascending channel and has continued to drop since September 2022. The index has formed strong support at the lower boundary of the channel near the 96 level and has been consolidating above this support zone since June 2025.
But the index broke above 100.50 in September and triggered a strong rally in October to reach a high at 102.945. This suggests a positive outlook. This rally was triggered by expectations of high interest rates in the coming months.
From technical perspective, the US dollar has remained uncertain since the lows of June 2025 and looks to find the next move. If the index drops back below 100.50, it will increase the possibility of another drop towards the support of ascending channel near 96.50.
As long as the 96 level holds in the US Dollar Index, the index may continue to consolidate near 104. However, if the index consolidates below 102 and breaks 96, it will increase the possibility of quick drop to 90.
A Break Above 102.80 Could Push Dollar to 106-107
The weekly chart for the US dollar index also shows that the recent drop in the index came from the 200-week SMA near 102. The index has already produced bearish weekly candle in October. Now it is consolidating in the near term to find the next move.
If the US dollar index continues to drop below 101.50, it will likely increase the possibility of a drop towards the 100.50 level. But a recovery above the 102.80 level will open the way for strong rally towards the descending trend line at the 106 to 107 level. This descending trend line stretches from the October 2022 highs.
EUR/USD Forecast: The Key Support at 1.11 Trigger Rebound
The chart below shows that the Federal Reserve increased interest rates to 4% in September 2026 while the ECB also increased the refinancing rate to 2.65%. This maintains the gap between the interest rates of these two banks. However, the higher interest rates at the Federal Reserve suggest strength in the US dollar, which has pushed EUR/USD to the downside.
The strong rally in the US dollar index in September has pushed EUR/USD towards the key support zone as seen in the chart below. The pair has already reached the $1.11 support as discussed in the previous analysis. The pair rebounded back towards the 1.1240 level.
If the pair continues to move above 1.1265, it will open the way for a rally to the 1.1360 level. For EUR/USD, the pair must break above the 1.16 level at the descending trend line to open the way for further upside towards the 1.19 level.
The strong support in EUR/USD is also observed on the daily chart which shows that the recent support near 1.11 was formed at the descending channel pattern. If EUR/USD holds 1.1130, it would likely rally towards the 50-day SMA near 1.1430. The pair will continue to consolidate in negative trend if it remains below the 200-day SMA at 1.1573.
GBP/USD Forecast: A Break Above 1.3430 Could Open the Path to 1.3650
The chart below shows that the Federal Reserve increased the interest rate to 4% in September, while the United Kingdom holds the interest rate at 3.75%. This increases the gap between the interest rates of these two banks by 0.25%. This further provides an advantage for US dollar against the pound.
However, GBP/USD has been trading within tight range of 1.30 to 1.3780 during the past year. This range has been narrowed to 1.3190 to 1.3650 since February 2026.
Now, the pair has formed strong support at 1.3190 in October 2026 and triggered a strong rally towards the 50-day SMA. A break above 1.3430 will likely continue the pair to the upside to 1.3650.
However, if the pair fails to hold the 1.33 level, it will trigger another drop towards 1.3190. Overall, the pair does not show any clear direction as the 50-day and 200-day moving averages are flat.
What to Watch Next
Oil prices broke the key levels last week and continued to surge, while AI spending remains strong. This can keep the cost of business high and strengthen the case for rate hike in December.
The weak employment data and slow growth could limit further gains in Treasury yields. I think that the next inflation and jobs data will help to understand whether the Fed needs to raise rates again. The correction in oil prices will likely ease that pressure.
The next move in US dollar will likely depend on how expectations for the Fed compare with expectations for the ECB and the Bank of England. A break above 102.80 in the US dollar index could strengthen the recovery, but a break below 100.50 would weaken the outlook for the US dollar.
A break above 102.80 in US dollar index may keep the EUR/USD under pressure in the short term. But a break above 1.1265 in the EUR/USD may extend the pair to 1.1360. On the other hand, a break above 1.3430 in GBP/USD may open the way for a rally to 1.3650.

high_priority_articles.title: How Brazil’s election could reshape relations with China - thenational.co.za
high_priority_articles.summary: How Brazil’s election could reshape relations with China  thenational.co.za
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Today, Brazilians will return to the polls to choose between President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who was sentenced to 27 years in prison for his role in an attempted coup.
The first round gave Flávio 47.03 per cent of valid votes against Lula’s 45.16 per cent, revealing the enduring strength of the far right four years after its electoral defeat.
The runoff takes place as Donald Trump seeks to restore US domination over Latin America, with Brazil emerging as a consequential battleground in Washington’s campaign to contain China’s growing relations with the region.
Over the past two decades, Brazil and China have built a political partnership that has expanded the space for independent action among countries of the Global South. Under Lula and Xi Jinping, this relationship has deepened through cooperation in industrial development, infrastructure, science, and technology.
The election will determine whether this project advances or Brazil’s international orientation is subordinated to Washington’s renewed Monroe Doctrine as part of the continent’s rightward shift.
Since Lula’s return to the presidency in 2023, the two governments have connected Chinese cooperation with Brazil’s development programmes. Lula’s May 2025 visit to Beijing produced 36 agreements covering infrastructure, finance, artificial intelligence, public health, and industrial cooperation.
Behind these agreements is a long-standing challenge: overcoming Brazil’s dependent position in the international division of labour, where commodity exports continue to outweigh advanced industrial and technological development. This cooperation has also reached Brazilian popular movements.
Brazil’s relationship with China also reveals the different class interests at work in the country, with contradictions particularly visible in the countryside. Massive exports of soybeans, meat, and minerals have continued under both Bolsonaro and Lula, but their governments have pursued very different political relationships with Beijing.
While Jair Bolsonaro attacked China and aligned himself with Washington, Lula has sought to deepen strategic cooperation, including in industrial development, technology, and agrarian reform.
Flávio Bolsonaro now promises an economically pragmatic relationship with China while cultivating close ties with Trump. For sectors of Brazil's ruling classes that profit from commodity exports, continuing to sell to China while embracing Washington's political agenda presents little contradiction.
For Brazil's efforts to rebuild its industry and develop technological sovereignty, the consequences are far greater.
The Return of the Monroe Doctrine
Washington’s ambitions were made explicit in its December 2025 National Security Strategy, which announced a ‘Trump Corollary’ to the Monroe Doctrine, seeking to restore US pre-eminence in the Western Hemisphere and deny outside powers control over strategic resources and infrastructure.
Five days later, China published its third Latin America policy paper, reaffirming sovereignty, non-interference, regional integration, technological cooperation, and support for the region as a Zone of Peace. The two documents reveal fundamentally different approaches to the political future of the continent.
Brazil’s position is decisive. As Latin America’s largest economy, a founding BRICS member, and a leading participant in Mercosur, it possesses industrial, scientific, and political capacities that could strengthen independent development across Latin America and beyond.
The emergence of a new technological era makes this struggle particularly consequential. Brazil is among the few countries of the Global South capable of pursuing digital and technological sovereignty that could benefit its neighbours and parts of Africa.
Its roughly 23 per cent share of global rare earth reserves is an important starting point, but control over minerals alone is insufficient. The greater challenge is developing the capacity to process them, manufacture advanced components, and build the digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence systems, and technologies that will shape future production.
Flávio has made his orientation clear. Speaking at the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) in the United States in March 2026, he offered Brazil as the ‘solution’ to Washington’s dependence on China for critical minerals, explicitly linking rare earths to artificial intelligence and US military superiority.
The same political orientation extends to digital sovereignty. In July 2026, Flávio’s campaign submitted proposals to US trade authorities that included preventing Brazil’s Pix payment system from connecting to non-Western international payment networks and loosening commitments within Mercosur.
These proposals converge with a wider US campaign involving tariffs, digital regulation, strategic minerals, and attempts to influence Brazil’s electoral process.
BRICS and the struggle for an independent foreign policy
Brazil, particularly under Lula, has helped build institutions through which countries of the Global South can reduce their dependence on Western-dominated structures.
At the July 2025 BRICS summit in Rio de Janeiro, the group advanced cooperation on development finance, local-currency transactions, and international institutional reform. The New Development Bank, headed by former Brazilian president Dilma Rousseff, is an important expression of this effort.
The BRICS cannot automatically overcome economic dependency or guarantee sovereignty for working people. Yet its expansion offers greater room for independent development, provided that participating governments have the political commitment to use these possibilities.
The international material conditions for South–South cooperation are considerably more favourable today, but political direction remains decisive. Jair Bolsonaro hosted the 2019 BRICS summit in Brasília while pursuing close alignment with Washington.
A government can weaken institutions from within by abandoning the commitments that give them political substance.
The far right’s resurgence also reflects the enduring power of Brazil’s own ruling classes. Their economic dependence on Chinese markets has not prevented their support for Washington’s political agenda.
Beyond the Election
Beijing has followed the Brazilian election closely, reflecting the importance of the political relationship built between Lula and Xi over years of cooperation. In July, Xi reaffirmed China's support for Brazil against external interference during a conversation with Lula.
China’s principle of non-interference means that the choice of Brazil’s government belongs to the Brazilian people, but Beijing’s diplomatic restraint should not be confused with an absence of political interests or an assumption that all governments would pursue the same relationship.
The experience of Jair Bolsonaro’s presidency has already shown the limits of commercial interests in sustaining a broader political partnership.
For the Brazilian people, the consequences extend well beyond foreign policy. The election will also shape the struggles over labour rights, public services, agrarian reform, and the defence of democratic space.
Brazil's renewed role in South–South cooperation under Lula has opened possibilities for a development project that responds to the needs of its working people, but realising those possibilities depends on the political and social forces capable of carrying it forward.
The Brazilian people have fought through dictatorship, neoliberal restructuring, parliamentary coups, and the rise of the far right to defend their political and social gains.
This election is another moment in that longer struggle, now unfolding amid renewed US imperial intervention and a transformation of the world’s technological foundations.
The future of China–Brazil cooperation will depend on the capacity of organised popular forces to build a sovereign national project and turn international cooperation into lasting changes in people’s lives.
* Chak is the Asia Co-Coordinator of Tricontinental: Institute for Social Research and an editor of the international edition of Wenhua Zongheng: A Journal of Contemporary Chinese Thought. This is an edited version of the article published at Globetrotter.
